newsitem.title: GERMANY: Falling water levels on Oder renew hope for dike.
newsitem.headline: Falling water levels on Oder renew hope for dike.

text.p: Thousands of German soldiers and volunteers were racing against the clock on Sunday, hoping to prop up a dike along the river Oder on the border to Poland long enough for floods to recede.

Should the dike break, which officials still say is likely, water would flood the Oderbruch basin, an area 17 km (11 miles) wide and 50 km (30 miles) long on Germany's frontier with Poland, engulfing villages, farms and factories.
"The situation remains critical," said a spokesman for the Brandenburg state interior ministry. "The biggest problem is that the water is receding so slowly."

The chances for success seemed to be improving, two weeks into a spectacular rescue effort which has seen the German army and a host of volunteers provide all the muscle and machinery they could muster to save the dikes in eastern Germany.

Further south in Ratzdorf, where the Oder and Neisse rivers that form Germany's eastern border meet, water levels have fallen some 14 cm (six inches) since Saturday, officials said, but the situation remains critical until the river falls further.
"We are hoping water levels will begin to fall faster," Brandenburg state environment minister Matthias Platzek told Germany's N-TV television.
"We hope to see the water recede 15 or 20 cm a day now and that would mean that we would begin to see the pressure on the dikes ease in just a couple of days."

More than 10,000 soldiers and thousands of aid workers, water rescue teams, volunteer firefighters and villagers have struggled for nearly two weeks to to keep dikes along the Oder river from bursting.
Germany has escaped the worst of a month of flooding that has killed more than 100 people in Poland and the Czech Republic, but damage to homes, businesses and farms has been extensive.
As long as water levels remain as high as they are now, pressing with the weight of some six tonnes against the sodden dikes, soldiers and aid workers remain on red alert.

For the past few days the army has used a new technique to dry out the sodden dikes. First divers laid a sheet of plastic six metres (40 feet) deep in the water and 100 metres (330 feet) long to prevent the water from seeping through the dike.
Then they placed a pipe along the 100-metre section of dike most vulnerable to breaking and began sucking the water out of the drenched foundations of the dam.

Repair work continues on a second line of dikes near Zollbruecke. Private builders delivered tonnes of gravel to build a five-metre wall as a second line of defence which officials hope will stop the flood should the main dike burst.

The last time a break in the dike flooded the Oderbruch region was in 1947 near Reitwein. The region lies below the level of the river, which presses against twists and turns in the dike as the Oder runs north to the Baltic Sea.
The Oderbruch basin was created 250 years ago by Frederick the Great of Prussia by draining swamps and redirecting the route of the Oder, gaining a huge valley of arable land.
Around 15,000 people have been evacuated from the region since last week and thousands more were warned to be ready to leave their homes at a moment's notice.
